title: Interior and Weather
premise: After their mother's funeral, Kestrel Dunmore returns to the family house to catalog her belongings and finds a notebook of lyrics in a handwriting that isn't hers — songs written by Ada Reyes, the mother's lifelong friend who vanished from the neighborhood decades ago. When one of the unrecorded songs plays on the radio, credited to someone else, Kestrel realizes the inheritance they've been sorting isn't money but silence: the story of two women whose love was folded into duty, betrayal, and an unfinished song. Following the last bus route to the old neighborhood before it's rerouted forever, Kestrel finds Ada alive in a care home, learns the truth of what their mother chose over love, and must decide whether to publish the songs — honoring truth at the cost of the mother's carefully guarded reputation. In the end, Kestrel records the final song with Ada's blessing and lets the house go, choosing loyalty to what actually happened over loyalty to the lie.
about_author: Noor Dunmore is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloging other people's letters before writing about the ones no one sends. They live near a decommissioned bus depot and write at the hour when the radio plays things it shouldn't.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Three days after the funeral, Kestrel begins cataloging the house room by room, practicing the eulogy they never gave aloud. The emotional beat is numb competence masking grief, ending when they find a locked cedar box under the floorboards of the sewing room.

chapters.title: Handwriting That Isn't Hers
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Inside the box: forty pages of lyrics, dated 1971–1979, signed A.R. Kestrel recognizes none of them but recognizes the intimacy in them. The beat is vertigo — the mother contained a stranger. Ends with a photograph of two young women laughing on a porch.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, with flashbacks. We learn Kestrel has spent five years drafting a letter to their mother about their own buried secret — a marriage ended, a name changed back — never sent. The parallel between mother and child crystallizes: silence as inheritance. Beat: recognition.

chapters.title: The Song on the Radio
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Driving home, a radio station plays 'Harbor Light' — word for word from the notebook — credited to a man named Gerald Voss. Kestrel pulls over, shaking. The beat is the past breaking into the present; the dead are not done speaking.

chapters.title: Gerald Voss, Songwriter
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Research reveals Voss, now famous and elderly, lived briefly in the old neighborhood in the seventies. His memoir mentions 'a talented friend who preferred anonymity.' The beat is cold anger — theft dressed as kindness.

chapters.title: The Last Bus Route
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The city announces the 42 line — the route to the old neighborhood — will be rerouted next month. Kestrel decides to go before the map erases the way there. Beat: resolve hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Porch Ghosts
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Walking the decaying neighborhood, Kestrel finds the porch from the photograph, meets Marisol, an aging neighbor who knew both women. Marisol goes quiet at Ada's name. Beat: the neighborhood remembers what the family buried.

chapters.title: Marisol's Version
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She recalls Ada Reyes, the music teacher everyone loved, and the mother, Ruth, who played piano like prayer. She remembers the summer everything changed but refuses to say what happened. Beat: warmth shadowed by a door closing.

chapters.title: Ada Reyes, Alive
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Marisol finally admits Ada lives in Fernwood Care Home, forty minutes out. Kestrel visits unannounced and finds a small woman with bright eyes who looks at them and says, 'You have Ruth's way of standing in doorways.' Beat: shock turning to tenderness.

chapters.title: What Ada Kept
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She tells Kestrel she wrote the songs for Ruth, and Ruth sang them only for her, in the closed shop after hours. She doesn't yet know they were recorded by anyone. Beat: love described plainly, without shame — a counterweight to decades of hiding.

chapters.title: The Summer of 1979
chapters.summary: Ada's POV, extended flashback. The two women's deepening bond, Ruth's engagement to Kestrel's father arranged by her family, and the night Ruth asked Ada to stop writing songs because 'they make it too true.' Beat: heartbreak as choice.

chapters.title: Gerald Enters
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Voss, then a charming traveling musician, heard Ruth singing through the shop window, charmed his way into their circle, and copied a notebook Ada lent Ruth. When confronted, he left town with the songs. Beat: betrayal, and Ruth's refusal to fight for them.

chapters.title: Why Ruth Stayed Silent
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ruth could have exposed Voss but didn't — exposure meant explaining why the songs mattered, who they were for. She chose her marriage, her child, her respectability. Ada chose exile. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of duty over love.

chapters.title: Kestrel's Confession
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Sitting with Ada, Kestrel finally says the thing unsaid for five years — about the marriage, the name, the letter never sent. Ada listens without flinching and says, 'Ruth almost said it too.' Beat: release; the generational knot loosening.

chapters.title: Voss Refuses
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel contacts Voss's estate lawyers demanding credit and royalties for Ada. Voss, dying but lucid, offers a settlement with a nondisclosure clause that would erase Ruth's role entirely. Beat: temptation — money and quiet versus truth.

chapters.title: The Rerouting
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The 42 line runs its final week. Kestrel rides it end to end with the notebook, reading the songs against the passing streets, understanding that the route itself was how Ruth visited Ada all those years without ever arriving. Beat: elegy for ordinary geography.

chapters.title: Ruth's Letter
chapters.summary: Mixed POV. In the cedar box's false bottom, Kestrel finds an unsent letter from Ruth to Ada, dated weeks before her death: an apology, and permission — 'Let them sing them. Let them know I was there.' Beat: the mother speaks at last, posthumously, and frees everyone.

chapters.title: The Offer Declined
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel rejects the settlement publicly, giving the notebook's story to a journalist. Voss's legacy cracks; some call Kestrel a betrayer of a dying man. Beat: cost made real — truth has a price, and Kestrel pays it willingly.

chapters.title: Recording Harbor Light
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In a small studio, Kestrel records 'Harbor Light' with Ada present, Ada humming the harmony Ruth once sang. The engineer asks who wrote it. Kestrel says both names. Beat: restoration — the song returned to its true shape.

chapters.title: Climax: The Reading of the Songs
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At a community hall on the old route, the songs are performed publicly; Marisol sings, Ada weeps, and Voss's family attends in stony silence until his daughter quietly admits she always suspected. Beat: catharsis — the neighborhood holds the whole truth at once, and no one shatters.

chapters.title: Emptying the House
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel sells the house, keeping only the piano and the photograph. The new owners, a young couple, ask about the sewing room floorboard. Kestrel says, 'Check under it.' Beat: inheritance redefined as something passed forward, not hoarded.

chapters.title: Interior and Weather
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, coda. A year later, Kestrel hears 'Harbor Light' on the radio, correctly credited, and pulls over again — this time to listen all the way through. The last bus has been rerouted, but Kestrel walks the old streets anyway. Beat: peace; the weather inside finally clearing.
